pedagogy.summary: Substitution is a procedure: replace each letter with its given value — keeping the operations the notation encodes — then evaluate using the correct order of operations. It is best taught by making the hidden multiplication and the protective brackets EXPLICIT: rewrite 3a as 3×a and always drop the substituted value inside brackets, e.g. 3×(5)² or (−2)², so that powers, signs and order of operations are handled correctly. Practise across a deliberate range of values — positive, zero, negative and fractional — because each exposes a different error.
bestPractices: Rewrite implicit operations before substituting: 3a becomes 3×a, a² becomes a×a — this pre-empts concatenation ('34') and the '×2' misreading of squaring.
Always substitute the value inside brackets, especially for negatives: (−2)² not −2², so two negatives making a positive is visible.
Contrast a² and 2a on the same value (a=5 gives 25 vs 10) so the child feels the difference.
Substitute a spread of values including 0 and negatives, and use a function machine or spreadsheet/table to generate many results and reveal patterns.
After substituting, treat the result as an ordinary arithmetic expression and apply order of operations (powers, then ×÷, then +−), boxing each term first.
keyRepresentations: Function machine / 'substitution machine' (value in, result out)
Area square for a² (a by a) contrasted with a bar of length 2a
Table/spreadsheet of values for one expression
Number line for negative substituted values
commonMisconceptions: Concatenation: substitutes to make digits, e.g. 3a with a=4 read as '34' instead of 3×4=12.
Reads a² as a×2, e.g. a² with a=5 evaluated as 10 rather than 25.
Ignores order of operations after substituting, e.g. 2+3a with a=4 done left-to-right as (2+3)×4=20 instead of 14.
Drops brackets on a negative value, e.g. (−2)² evaluated as −4 instead of 4 (−x² vs (−x)² confusion).
Assumes a=0 makes every term vanish, forgetting constants.

learn.summary: Substitution is a procedure: replace each letter with its given value, keep the operations the notation encodes, then evaluate using the correct order of operations. Make the hidden multiplication and the protective brackets explicit — rewrite 3a as 3×a and place every substituted value inside brackets, e.g. 3×(5)² or (−2)² — so powers, signs and order of operations are handled correctly. Practise across a deliberate spread of values (positive, zero, negative and fractional), and transfer the same discipline to an unfamiliar formula, because each value and each new formula exposes a different error.

activities.title: Rebuild-the-expression substitution with a sliding value
feedback: If a value and coefficient are written side by side as digits (e.g. 3a with a=4 read as '34'), re-establish that 3a means 3×a by expanding 3a as a+a+a for a small value, then rewrite with explicit × signs before substituting.
If a² with a=5 is evaluated as 10, contrast a² and 2a at a=5 (25 vs 10): rewrite a² as a×a explicitly, and compare a 5-by-5 area square with a bar of length 10.
If a negative gives (−2)² = −4 or the bracket is dropped as −2², write (−2)×(−2) in full, link to two negatives making a positive, and contrast −2² with (−2)² side by side.
If operations are taken left-to-right (e.g. 2+3a with a=4 done as (2+3)×4=20 instead of 14), the substitution itself was fine — box each term first, then resolve powers, then ×÷, then +−.
activities.rationale: Substitution is a procedure built by repeated doing with feedback across a range of values; making the implicit multiplication and the protective brackets explicit pre-empts the concatenation, squaring-as-doubling, sign and order-of-operations errors that are documented when pupils interpret and evaluate algebraic notation.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions, including scientific formulae, and use conventional algebraic notation (3y, a² etc.).

Students misread algebraic notation — e.g. treating 3a as concatenation rather than 3×a — and apply operations left-to-right rather than by order of operations when interpreting/evaluating expressions.
Students assume −(x²) is the same as (−x)², e.g. classifying x²+4=0 as true at x=−2 — the documented negative-square/sign error that shows up when substituting negative values.
Reading a² as doubling and letter-as-object interpretations are persistent, documented difficulties among 11–16 year-olds that resurface during substitution.
learnerActions: Take the expression 3a² − 2a and first rewrite the implicit operations explicitly: 3×a×a − 2×a, or 3×(a)² − 2×(a).
Choose a value for a and drop it inside the brackets so the expression becomes 3×( )² − 2×( ), e.g. 3×(5)² − 2×(5).
Evaluate in order: resolve the power first, then the multiplications, then the subtraction. For a=5: 3×25 − 10 = 75 − 10 = 65.
Repeat the same expression for a sequence of values — try a = 3, then a = 0, then a = −2, then a = 1/2 — writing out every step each time.
For each value, note alongside what the two parts (a² and 2a) came to separately, and watch how a² stays non-negative while 2a goes negative as a crosses zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Substitution means replacing the letter with its value while preserving the encoded operations; brackets protect negatives so (−2)² = +4, and a² (=a×a) behaves differently from 2a (=2×a).

activities.title: Contrast a² against 2a on the same value
feedback: If the learner still reads the exponent as a doubling coefficient, return to a×a written in full and the area-square picture before trying another value.
If they claim a² and 2a are always different, prompt them to test a=0 and a=2, where the two happen to coincide, so the generalisation is tested rather than assumed.
activities.rationale: Directly contrasting a² and 2a on shared values targets the persistent 'square as doubling' misinterpretation; an area model makes the a×a meaning concrete.
sourceClaims: Reading a² as doubling and letter-as-object interpretations are persistent, documented difficulties among 11–16 year-olds that resurface during substitution.
learnerActions: Pick a value, e.g. a=5, and evaluate a² and 2a separately: a² = 5×5 = 25, 2a = 2×5 = 10.
Draw a 5-by-5 square for a² next to a bar of length 10 for 2a, and compare their sizes.
Repeat for a=0 (both give 0) and for a=3, recording how the two results diverge.
State in your own words why a² and 2a are generally not the same, and identify when they do coincide.
activities.intendedInsight: a² means a×a, not a×2; the exponent is not a coefficient, so the two expressions generally give very different values (coinciding only at a=0 and a=2).

activities.title: Negative and fractional values that expose the rules
feedback: If (−2)² comes out as −4, rewrite it as (−2)×(−2) and connect to two negatives multiplying to a positive; contrast −2² with (−2)² explicitly.
For −a², if the sign flips between a=3 and a=−3, point out that the square is taken first and is always non-negative, so the leading minus gives −9 in both cases.
If a=0 makes the learner zero out a constant term, point back to the constant and ask what it equals when nothing is multiplied by a.
activities.rationale: Negative, zero and fractional values each trigger a distinct documented error; deliberately sampling them while insisting on brackets and order of operations surfaces and corrects the sign and over-generalisation mistakes.
sourceClaims: Students assume −(x²) is the same as (−x)², e.g. classifying x²+4=0 as true at x=−2 — the documented negative-square/sign error that shows up when substituting negative values.
learnerActions: Evaluate 3a² − 2a at a = −2, substituting inside brackets: 3×(−2)² − 2×(−2) = 3×4 + 4 = 12 + 4 = 16.

Evaluate −a² at a = 3 and at a = −3, substituting inside brackets (−(3)² and −(−3)²), and check that BOTH give −9; then evaluate (−a)² at the same values, (−3)² and (3)², which both give +9 — confirming −a² differs from (−a)².
Evaluate the expression at a = 1/2, keeping the fraction inside the bracket for the square and ordering the operations correctly.
Try a = 0 and check each term explicitly, including any constant, instead of assuming everything vanishes.
Optionally use a number line to place each negative substituted value and keep track of its sign before applying the power.
activities.intendedInsight: Brackets around a substituted value preserve its sign under powers, so (−2)² = 4; −a² and (−a)² are different; and special values like 0 and fractions must still be evaluated term by term with correct order of operations.

activities.title: Check and talk-through across error-triggering values
feedback: Build comparison options from documented errors — e.g. 34 (concatenation), 10 (square read as doubling) — and ask the learner to identify and correct each.
If the correct final value is reached but a step is skipped, ask for the intermediate power and product values to check the reasoning, not just the answer.

If the method breaks down on the unfamiliar formula (e.g. v = u + a×t evaluated left-to-right as (3+2)×4 = 20 instead of 11), re-apply the box-each-term rule — multiplication before addition — to the substituted formula, showing the substitution itself was fine.
activities.rationale: Checking performance across the error-triggering values and extending to an unfamiliar formula confirms fluency and transfer; using documented wrong answers as discussion points turns common errors into teaching moments. A completion/selection check confirms the procedure but, on its own, elicits less independent step-by-step construction than open working, so pair it with talk-through.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions, including scientific formulae, and use conventional algebraic notation (3y, a² etc.).

Students misread algebraic notation — e.g. treating 3a as concatenation rather than 3×a — and apply operations left-to-right rather than by order of operations when interpreting/evaluating expressions.
Reading a² as doubling and letter-as-object interpretations are persistent, documented difficulties among 11–16 year-olds that resurface during substitution.
learnerActions: Given 3a² − 2a, complete the partially-worked line 3×(5)² − 2×(5) = __, showing the power step, the multiplication step and the subtraction step.
For a second expression such as 3a − 1, find its value when a = 4 and explain each step.

Transfer the same procedure to an unfamiliar formula with given values — e.g. find v in v = u + a×t when u = 3, a = 2, t = 4, giving v = 3 + 2×4 = 3 + 8 = 11 — to confirm the discipline carries beyond the practised expression.
Explain why a wrong value such as 34 (for 3a with a=4) or 10 (for a² with a=5) is incorrect, naming the mistake.
When finished, point to the step where the power was worked out and talk through just that step to show the order-of-operations reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluating at given values, transferring the method to an unfamiliar formula, and explaining why common wrong answers are wrong consolidates the correct procedure and reveals whether order of operations and notation are genuinely understood.

constraints: Choose an expression that contains BOTH a square and a coefficient, e.g. 3a² − 2a, so the a² vs 2a distinction and the sign rules both come into play.
Always substitute the value inside brackets, especially for negatives — (−2)² not −2² — so the sign is protected.
After substituting, treat the result as an ordinary arithmetic expression and apply order of operations (powers, then ×÷, then +−), boxing each term first.

Deliberately sample positive, zero, negative and fractional values; each exposes a different error, and the negative case is decisive because it requires keeping the bracket AND knowing two negatives multiply to a positive.
Include transfer to at least one unfamiliar formula (the curriculum scope covers scientific formulae) so the procedure is shown to generalise beyond the practised expression.

A completion or selection check (fill-in-the-blank, set-the-value, or pick-the-answer with distractors like 34 and 10) confirms the procedure but does not by itself elicit independent step-by-step construction; pair it with open working and talk-through.
A tap-to-reveal worked example can show one substitution's steps as a scaffold, but the learner still needs to perform the procedure across several values to build fluency.

Live manipulation (sliding a value through positive, zero and negative while the expression auto-rebuilds and brackets snap around the value) is an optional way to make the a² vs 2a difference and the (−2)²=+4 behaviour visible; it is one helpful presentation, not a required mechanism, and the same learning can be reached with written working, a number line for negatives, or a table/spreadsheet of values.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (Hodgen, Küchemann, Brown & Coe 2009) is marked unverified in the row; treat its 'reading a² as doubling' claim with corresponding caution.

Self-audit of arithmetic: a=5 gives 3×25 − 10 = 65; a=−2 gives 3×4 + 4 = 16; −a² at a=3 and a=−3 both give −9; a²=2a only at a=0 and a=2; transfer example v = u + a×t with u=3,a=2,t=4 gives 3 + 8 = 11. All checked and retained.

The original catalog fit-rankings claiming dialogue 'cannot efficiently' teach the procedure, that a static image 'cannot let the child DO the procedure', and that a third dimension 'adds nothing' were comparative-efficacy assertions, not established evidence; they have been removed or softened to scope-limited statements about affordances.

The gap description (notation misread so no correct value is produced) and the distinction between substitution errors and order-of-operations errors are preserved as feedback branches; an order-of-operations error after substitution does not require reteaching substitution.

Source-claim attachments were tightened: the MAP concatenation/order claim was kept only where the relevant errors are actually addressed; the generic KS3 claim was attached to the core substitution activity and the transfer-to-formula step, not to the a²-vs-2a or the negative/fractional-value activities whose principles it does not directly support.

A transfer step to an unfamiliar formula was added to the check activity to honour the objective's 'including scientific formulae' scope and the assessment's 'full' transfer criterion, which the earlier candidate had dropped; this addition is a proposal, not an empirically validated task.

probeDeeper: Now find it for a = 0 — watch whether they still evaluate each term or assume '0 makes everything 0' and forget the constant behaviour. (counterexample: a special value that tempts over-generalisation)
Change it to −a² and do a = 3 and a = −3 — watch whether BOTH give −9 (correct) or whether the sign flips between them. (counterexample separating −a² from (−a)²)
Give a = 1/2 and watch whether they can substitute a fraction into the square and still order the operations.
After they finish, point to the step where they worked out the power and say 'talk me through just that step' — surfaces their order-of-operations reasoning without having pre-cued it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Concatenation — substitutes to form digits rather than multiply, e.g. treats 3a as '34' when a=4, or writes the coefficient beside the value.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to notation: 3a means 3×a. Re-establish by expanding 3a as a+a+a for a small value, then rewrite the expression with explicit × signs before substituting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes the coefficient and the substituted value side by side as a multi-digit number instead of multiplying (e.g. 3a² with a=5 becomes 3 then 25 written as '325' or similar).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a² as a×2, e.g. a² with a=5 evaluated as 10 rather than 25.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a² and 2a with a=5 (25 vs 10) using an area square (5 by 5) beside a bar of length 10; rewrite a² as a×a explicitly before substituting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 5×2=10 (or 3×10) where the square is required; treats the exponent as a coefficient.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores order of operations after substituting — works left-to-right, e.g. does the subtraction or the multiplication before the power.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT reteach substitution — the substitution was fine. Reteach order of operations on the resulting numerical expression: box each term first, resolve powers, then ×÷, then ±.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Squares last, or evaluates 2+3a as (2+3)×4; the written steps show operations taken in reading order rather than powers→×÷→+−.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles a negative value — (−2)² evaluated as −4, or the bracket is dropped giving −2² = −4 (−x² vs (−x)² confusion).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on substituting inside brackets always; write (−2)×(−2) in full and connect to two-negatives-make-a-positive; contrast −2² with (−2)² explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a=−2 writes (−2)²=−4, or drops the bracket entirely; the a=−2 answer comes out negative or otherwise wrong while a=5 was right.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot begin, or the substitution is meaningless because notation is misread — concatenates (34 for 3a with a=4) or reads the square as doubling, so no correct value is produced.
responseLevels.full: Substitutes positive AND negative values, handles powers and multi-operation expressions with correct order of operations, protects negatives with brackets so (−2)²=4, and transfers the same discipline to an unfamiliar formula.
responseLevels.partial: Substitutes correctly for a positive whole number with straightforward operations (gets the a=5 case right), but breaks down on the a=−2 case, on the power, or on order of operations — handles the routine value but not the ones that expose a rule.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child this card and say 'work these out, thinking aloud, and show every step': Find the value of 3a² − 2a when a = 5, and then when a = −2. Say NOTHING about method — watch the order they compute, how they handle the square, and how they deal with the negative.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the teacher WATCHES rather than asks, each error surfaces as a different visible line of working: a child who concatenates writes 35 for 3a²; one who reads the square as ×2 writes 3×10; one who ignores order of operations squares last or subtracts first; one who mishandles the negative writes (−2)²=−4 or drops the bracket. The a=−2 case is decisive — it cannot be got right by a child who does not both keep the bracket and know two negatives multiply to a positive.
